q: Corals stay fixed to the seafloor like plants. What are they actually?
explain: Corals are invertebrate animals. They look plant-like because they are anchored in place, but unlike plants they do not make their own food by photosynthesis.

source.title: Are corals animals, plants, or something else? - NOAA Ocean Exploration

source2.title: What Is Coral? A Coral Polyp and Zooxanthellae

searchNote: NOAA Ocean Exploration says corals are invertebrate animals in phylum Cnidaria, often mistaken for plants because they are attached to the seafloor; they do not photosynthesize themselves.

q: What is each of the many tiny individual animals that make up a coral colony called?
explain: What we call a coral is usually hundreds or thousands of small animals called polyps, living together as one colony.

source.title: Are corals animals, plants, or something else? - NOAA Ocean Exploration

source2.title: What Is Coral? A Coral Polyp and Zooxanthellae

searchNote: NOAA says a coral is made up of hundreds to thousands of individual animals called polyps.

q: Corals belong to the phylum Cnidaria. Which of these animals is also in that group?
explain: Corals share the phylum Cnidaria with jellyfish and sea anemones, animals that all carry stinging cells.

source.title: Are corals animals, plants, or something else? - NOAA Ocean Exploration

searchNote: NOAA Ocean Exploration places corals in phylum Cnidaria and says they share it with sea anemones and jellies.

q: What are the zooxanthellae that live inside reef-building corals?
explain: Zooxanthellae are microscopic algae living in coral tissue. They photosynthesize and pass food to the coral, which gives them shelter in return.

source.title: Corals Tutorial: Zooxanthellae purpose

source2.title: What Is Coral? A Coral Polyp and Zooxanthellae

searchNote: NOAA's corals tutorial and Smithsonian Ocean describe zooxanthellae as single-celled algae living in coral tissue that supply the coral with food made by photosynthesis.

q: Up to roughly what share of the food made by a coral's zooxanthellae is passed to the coral?
explain: NOAA estimates that as much as 90 percent of the organic material the algae make by photosynthesis goes to the host coral's tissue.

source.title: NOAA National Ocean Service Education: Corals

searchNote: NOAA corals tutorial says as much as 90 percent of the organic material produced photosynthetically by zooxanthellae is transferred to the coral tissue. (A Smithsonian-linked source cites up to 95%, also far from the distractors.)

q: Where does most of the color of a reef-building coral come from?
explain: The zooxanthellae algae in coral tissue supply much of a coral's color. That is why corals that lose them turn pale or white.

source.title: What is coral bleaching?

source2.title: Zooxanthellae and Coral Bleaching

searchNote: NOAA's coral bleaching page says the algae living in coral tissue give corals their color; without them the white skeleton shows.

q: What is the most common cause of coral bleaching?
explain: When water gets too warm, stressed corals expel the algae living in their tissues and turn white. Changes in light or nutrients can also trigger it.

source.title: What is coral bleaching?

source2.title: Zooxanthellae and Coral Bleaching

searchNote: NOAA says corals stressed by changes in temperature, light or nutrients expel their symbiotic algae, and that warm water is the most common cause.

q: What is true of a coral that has just bleached white?
choices: It has become a new species
explain: A bleached coral is not dead and can recover if conditions improve. If bleaching is severe or lasts too long, though, the coral can die.

source.title: What is coral bleaching?

searchNote: NOAA says a bleached coral is not dead and can survive bleaching, but becomes more vulnerable and may die if the stress is prolonged.

q: Besides heat, which of these has caused coral bleaching in the Florida Keys?
explain: Bleaching is a stress response, and cold snaps can trigger it too. A cold-water event in the Florida Keys bleached corals and killed some of them.

source.title: Florida Keys NMS: Coral Bleaching

source2.title: What is coral bleaching?

q: Many reef corals spawn by releasing eggs and sperm in what form?
explain: Many spawning corals pack eggs and sperm together into small buoyant bundles. These float to the surface and break apart so eggs can be fertilized.

source.publisher: NOAA Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary
source.title: Coral Spawning

source2.title: Coral Spawning

searchNote: NOAA Flower Garden Banks says many hermaphroditic broadcast spawners release bundles of eggs and sperm that float to the surface and break apart.

q: At the Flower Garden Banks in the Gulf, when does the main coral spawning usually happen?
choices: 1 to 2 nights before August's full moon
7 to 10 nights after August's full moon
About 30 nights after August's full moon
explain: Spawning there is tied to the moon. Different species release eggs and sperm on different nights in the week or so after the August full moon.

source.publisher: NOAA Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary
source.title: Spawning Observations

searchNote: NOAA Flower Garden Banks spawning observations say the main event occurs about seven to ten nights after the August full moon, with species spawning on different nights.

q: Elkhorn coral in the Caribbean spawns for just a few nights each summer. At about what time?
explain: Elkhorn coral spawns on only a few summer nights after a full moon, typically about three hours after sunset, so researchers must be ready to collect it.

source.title: Spawning Hope

searchNote: Smithsonian's National Zoo says elkhorn coral spawns only a few nights each summer after a full moon, typically about three hours after sunset.

q: Some coral species are 'gonochoric.' What does that mean?
choices: Each colony is either male or female
explain: In gonochoric corals, female colonies release egg bundles and male colonies release clouds of sperm, rather than each colony making both.

source.publisher: NOAA Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary
source.title: Coral Spawning

searchNote: NOAA Flower Garden Banks says some species are gonochoric: female colonies release egg bundles while male colonies release sperm.

q: What is a free-swimming coral larva called?
explain: A fertilized coral egg develops into a tiny larva called a planula, which drifts and swims until it finds a place to settle and become a polyp.

source.title: NOAA National Ocean Service Education: Corals Tutorial

source2.title: Coral Reproduction - Coral Disease & Health Consortium

searchNote: NOAA corals tutorial and the NOAA CDHC reproduction page describe coral larvae as planulae that settle and metamorphose into polyps.

q: What is thought to be the strongest cue telling a coral larva where to settle?
explain: Larvae respond to several signals, but a chemical released by certain crusty, pink coralline algae is considered the most potent settlement cue.

source.title: Coral Reproduction - Coral Disease & Health Consortium

searchNote: NOAA CDHC says a variety of cues guide larvae to suitable substrate, and the most potent is a chemical signal released by certain crustose coralline algae.

q: In experiments, settling coral larvae moved toward which reef cue?
choices: Reef sounds from fish and shrimp
explain: Larvae swam toward recorded reef sounds made mainly by fish and crustaceans. It was the first known hearing-type response in the coral and jellyfish group.

source.title: Coral Larvae Move toward Reef Sounds

searchNote: PLOS ONE study: settling coral larvae were attracted to reef sounds produced mainly by fish and crustaceans, the first auditory response described in Cnidaria.

q: For most coral species, how soon do larvae settle after spawning?
explain: Most coral larvae settle within a couple of days, though some swim for up to three weeks before choosing a spot.

source.title: Coral Reproduction - Coral Disease & Health Consortium

searchNote: NOAA CDHC says in most species larvae settle within two days, though some swim for up to three weeks, and one known case two months.

q: Compared with broadcast-spawned larvae, larvae released by brooding corals usually do what?
choices: Settle sooner and nearer the parent
explain: Brooding corals keep developing young inside, so their larvae are released ready to settle quickly and tend to land close to the parent colony.

source.title: Coral Reproduction - Coral Disease & Health Consortium

searchNote: NOAA CDHC says brooding species release larvae that are ready to settle sooner and usually settle closer to the parent colony.

q: How does a coral larva's swimming speed compare with the water currents around reefs?
explain: A review found coral larvae swim orders of magnitude slower than reef water flow, so they have very little ability to steer themselves to a settling spot.

source.title: Coral larvae are poor swimmers and require fine-scale reef structure to settle

searchNote: Peer-reviewed meta-analysis: coral larval swimming speeds are orders of magnitude lower than water flow on and off reefs, so navigation ability is extremely limited.

q: A broken piece of coral reattaches and keeps growing. What is this an example of?
explain: Corals can reproduce asexually by budding new polyps or by fragmentation, when a broken piece survives and grows into a new colony.

source.title: NOAA National Ocean Service Education: Corals Tutorial

searchNote: NOAA corals tutorial reproduction page describes asexual reproduction in corals by budding and by fragmentation of broken pieces.

q: What do stony corals build their hard skeletons from?
explain: Each stony coral polyp secretes a skeleton of calcium carbonate. Over many generations these skeletons build the massive structure of a reef.

source.title: What is a coral reef made of?

source2.publisher: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary
source2.title: Coral Reefs - Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary - NOAA

searchNote: NOAA Ocean Service says reef structures form when each stony coral polyp secretes a skeleton of calcium carbonate.

q: When do most coral polyps stretch out their tentacles to feed?
explain: Most coral polyps feed at night, emerging from their skeletons to snag drifting zooplankton. By day, many rely on food from their algae.

source.title: Coral Reefs - Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary - NOAA

source2.title: NOAA National Ocean Service Education: Corals

searchNote: NOAA Florida Keys and the NOAA corals tutorial say most polyps feed at night, coming out of their skeletons to catch floating prey.

q: What do coral polyps use to capture prey such as zooplankton?
explain: Coral tentacles carry stinging cells called nematocysts. When prey brushes against them, they fire and help hold the food.

source2.publisher: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary
source2.title: Coral Reefs - Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary - NOAA

q: Besides catching prey with tentacles, how can some corals collect fine food particles?
explain: Some corals produce mucus that traps fine bits of organic matter, which they then draw into their mouths.

source.title: NOAA National Ocean Service Education: Corals

q: Deep-sea corals such as Lophelia live where sunlight does not reach. How do they get food?
choices: Using algae that glow in the dark
explain: Deep-sea corals do not host the sunlight-using algae of shallow reefs. They feed on plankton and organic matter sinking from above or carried by currents.

q: How many tentacles does each polyp of a soft coral (octocoral) have?
explain: Soft corals are also called octocorals because each polyp has eight tentacles, which are often feathery.

q: Stony coral polyps grow tentacles in multiples of which number?

source.title: Coral Reefs - Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary - NOAA

q: Instead of rigid limestone, what supports soft corals such as sea fans?
explain: Sea fans and similar soft corals have a bendable internal skeleton built around gorgonin, a tough protein, which lets them sway in currents.

source.title: Coral Reefs - Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary - NOAA

q: Black corals are often mistaken for soft corals. How many tentacles do their polyps have?
explain: Despite looking like soft corals, black corals are hexacorals with six tentacles per polyp, unlike the eight-tentacled octocorals.

source.title: Species identification of Australian Museum black corals - The Australian Museum

q: Fire coral is a stinging reef builder. What kind of animal is it?
choices: A hydrozoan, not a true coral
explain: Fire corals build hard skeletons like corals but are hydrozoans, a different cnidarian class. Their name comes from their painful sting.

q: Corals and sea anemones belong to which class of animals?
explain: Corals and sea anemones are grouped together in the class Anthozoa, a name meaning 'flower animals.' Jellyfish and hydroids belong to other classes.

q: Which type of coral reef is the most common?
explain: Fringing reefs grow seaward directly from the shore, bordering coastlines and islands. They are the most common of the three main reef types.

source.title: What are the three main types of coral reefs?

searchNote: NOAA says the three main types are fringing, barrier and atoll, and fringing reefs are the most common, growing seaward directly from shore.

q: What is a ring-shaped coral reef with an open lagoon in the middle called?
explain: An atoll forms when a reef keeps growing upward around a volcanic island that slowly sinks, leaving a ring of reef around a central lagoon.

source.title: What are the three main types of coral reefs?

searchNote: NOAA says atolls are rings of coral around a central lagoon, formed when a fringing reef keeps growing up from a volcanic island that subsides.

q: What separates a barrier reef from the shore?
explain: Barrier reefs sit farther from land than fringing reefs, with a lagoon of open, often deep water between the reef and the coast.

source.title: What are the three main types of coral reefs?

searchNote: NOAA says barrier reefs are separated from the shore by a lagoon of open, often deep water.

q: Who proposed that reefs develop from fringing reef to barrier reef to atoll as volcanic islands sink?
explain: Charles Darwin's subsidence theory linked the three reef types in one sequence, with reefs growing upward as the islands they surround slowly sink.

source2.title: What are the three main types of coral reefs?

Up to about 10 cm a year

An empty strip with no anemones
